title: The software supply chain threat model and SLSA
summary: How the parts of this lesson fit together.

steps.n: Code is written and reviewed, dependencies are pulled, a build runs, an image is pushed to a registry, a deployment tool pulls it and the cluster runs it.

Examples include a malicious or hijacked dependency, a stolen CI token that pushes a poisoned image, a tag that is moved to a different image, a compromised build runner and an unreviewed change merged by a bot.
SLSA, the supply chain levels for software artifacts, describes how trustworthy a build is.
Provenance is a signed statement: this image digest was built from this commit by this pipeline at this time.
Pin images by digest, scan dependencies, require reviews, protect the main branch and use short lived credentials in CI.
Confirm the outcome with a metric, a query or a test, and write down what changed so the next person can repeat it.

title: Failure and recovery: The tag that changed after review
summary: A realistic failure and the way back.

steps.n: The system works and the team relies on it, so nobody is watching this particular risk closely.
A deployment pulled a latest tag that pointed to an image nobody had reviewed.
An operator runs a command such as: kubectl get pod web-1 -o jsonpath='{.status.containerStatuses[0].imageID}'
The tag 1.8 had been moved to a new image after the review, so the running digest did not match the reviewed one.
The team pinned deployments by digest, made tags immutable in the registry and added a check that compares the deployed digest to the one in the release record.
The team closes the gap: avoid this mistake: Deploying mutable tags such as latest.
The incident is reviewed for system and process causes and the runbook is updated so the next responder finds the answer faster.

title: Image scanning and vulnerability management
summary: How the parts of this lesson fit together.

steps.n: Tools such as Trivy compare package versions in the image to vulnerability databases.
Most findings come from the operating system packages in the base image.
Severity alone is not enough. This keeps the next step safe and easy to check.
Fail a pipeline on fixable critical and high findings that apply to the runtime image.
When you cannot fix something, record the reason, the owner and an expiry date.
Confirm the outcome with a metric, a query or a test, and write down what changed so the next person can repeat it.

title: Failure and recovery: A critical finding two weeks after release
summary: A realistic failure and the way back.

steps.n: The system works and the team relies on it, so nobody is watching this particular risk closely.
A library vulnerability was published after the image shipped and nobody noticed.
An operator runs a command such as: trivy image --severity CRITICAL,HIGH --ignore-unfixed registry.example.com/api@sha256:41be0d20
The image had no scheduled rescan, so the new finding only appeared during a manual check.
A nightly rescan job now opens a ticket for the owning team, and the base image is rebuilt weekly so most fixes arrive without effort.
The team closes the gap: avoid this mistake: Failing builds on every low severity finding.
The incident is reviewed for system and process causes and the runbook is updated so the next responder finds the answer faster.

title: SBOMs, signing and verification with cosign
summary: How the parts of this lesson fit together.

steps.n: An SBOM lists the packages and versions in an image, in formats such as SPDX or CycloneDX.
Cosign signs the image digest and stores the signature next to the image in the registry.
Keyless signing uses a short lived certificate issued to the identity of the CI job, such as a workflow in a repository, through OpenID Connect.
Verification checks that a signature exists for the digest and that the signer identity and issuer match what you expect.
If you use keys, keep them in a KMS or hardware module and rotate them.
Confirm the outcome with a metric, a query or a test, and write down what changed so the next person can repeat it.

title: Failure and recovery: A signed image from the wrong workflow
summary: A realistic failure and the way back.

steps.n: The system works and the team relies on it, so nobody is watching this particular risk closely.
An image signed by a test workflow was promoted to production.
An operator runs a command such as: cosign verify registry.example.com/api@sha256:41be0d20 --certificate-identity-regexp 'https://github.com/examp
The identity pattern accepted any workflow in the organisation, including a test workflow.
The policy was tightened to the release workflow on the main branch, and the verification step now fails for any other identity.
The team closes the gap: avoid this mistake: Signing tags instead of digests.
The incident is reviewed for system and process causes and the runbook is updated so the next responder finds the answer faster.

title: Admission enforcement of provenance with policy
summary: How the parts of this lesson fit together.

steps.n: Useful rules include: images must come from approved registries, must be referenced by digest, must have a valid signature from the release identity and must have an SBOM or provenance attestation.
Kyverno expresses policies as Kubernetes resources and has built in image verification.
Start in audit mode, which records violations without blocking.
Some system namespaces and vendor images need exceptions.
A policy webhook with failure policy fail blocks changes when it is down, and with ignore it lets everything through.
Confirm the outcome with a metric, a query or a test, and write down what changed so the next person can repeat it.

title: Failure and recovery: Enforce mode that blocked a security patch
summary: A realistic failure and the way back.

steps.n: The system works and the team relies on it, so nobody is watching this particular risk closely.
A fix could not be deployed because its new image was not signed yet.
An operator runs a command such as: kubectl apply -f deploy.yaml
The build pipeline had signed images only on the main branch, but the patch came from a release branch.
The pipeline was fixed to sign release branches, and the team used a time limited exception to ship the urgent patch while the fix was in review.
The team closes the gap: avoid this mistake: Switching to enforce without an audit period.
The incident is reviewed for system and process causes and the runbook is updated so the next responder finds the answer faster.

title: Runtime detection with Falco and audit events
summary: How the parts of this lesson fit together.

steps.n: Falco watches system calls through an eBPF probe or a kernel module and matches them against rules.

Start with rules for a shell started inside a container, a write below system directories, reading of service account tokens by unexpected processes, outbound connections to unusual ports and use of package managers in running containers.
The API server audit log records who did what through the API: secret reads, exec into pods, role changes.
Every cluster has legitimate shells and package managers, such as debug sessions or build jobs.
Send alerts with the pod, namespace, image and rule name to a channel or ticket system.
Confirm the outcome with a metric, a query or a test, and write down what changed so the next person can repeat it.

title: Failure and recovery: A shell in the payments pod
summary: A realistic failure and the way back.

steps.n: The system works and the team relies on it, so nobody is watching this particular risk closely.
Falco reported a shell started in a production container at night.
An operator runs a command such as: kubectl logs -n falco ds/falco | grep payments | head -2
The shell ran from a vulnerable endpoint that accepted a command.
The pod was quarantined with a deny network policy, evidence was copied, the image was patched and a rule for outbound connections from this namespace was added.
The team closes the gap: avoid this mistake: Disabling a noisy rule instead of adding a scoped exception.
The incident is reviewed for system and process causes and the runbook is updated so the next responder finds the answer faster.

title: Sandboxing: seccomp, AppArmor and runtime classes
summary: How the parts of this lesson fit together.

steps.n: A container is a process with namespaces and cgroups.
Seccomp filters system calls. This keeps the next step safe and easy to check.
These mandatory access control systems restrict files and operations per process.
Drop all Linux capabilities and add back only what is needed, run as non-root, disallow privilege escalation and set the root file system read only.
A RuntimeClass selects a runtime for a pod, for example gVisor or Kata Containers.
Confirm the outcome with a metric, a query or a test, and write down what changed so the next person can repeat it.

title: Failure and recovery: A seccomp profile that broke a release
summary: A realistic failure and the way back.

steps.n: The system works and the team relies on it, so nobody is watching this particular risk closely.
A custom profile blocked a system call the new library used.
An operator runs a command such as: kubectl logs api-5c8 | tail -2
The profile had been recorded before a library upgrade and missed a new call.
The team switched to RuntimeDefault for the release, re-recorded the custom profile in a test environment and added a test that runs the app with the profile in CI.
The team closes the gap: avoid this mistake: Leaving seccomp unconfined.
The incident is reviewed for system and process causes and the runbook is updated so the next responder finds the answer faster.
